To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

intestinal lamina propria CD4+ T cells are unresponsive to antigenic stimulation because of a limited capacity of the lamina propria to produce the essential thiol, cysteine, which is required for cell cycle progression and proliferation of these cells.

the low proliferative capacity of intestinal lamina propria CD4+ T cells is due to a low intracellular concentration of the antioxidant glutathione, and that the low concentration of glutathione is a direct consequence of the low capacity of lamina propria antigen-presenting cells, in particular monocytes, to reduce the disulfide bond in cystine to the thiol in cysteine.

cysteine is essential for proliferation of lamina propria CD4+ T cells, that cysteine release by antigen-presenting cells is a critical parameter for the proliferation of lamina The intestinal lamina propria contains a high number of T lymphocytes, but these T cells have a markedly low proliferation potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel mechanism of T cell activation, which may be important in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (1).
the identification of a novel regulatory mechanism that controls the proliferative potential of LP-Ts and may represent a critical factor in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease.
redox regulation of T cell function and the role of this mechanism in the intestinal immune response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the capacity of intestinal APCs to provide cysteine is a critical parameter for the reactivity of LP T cells and that this capacity is lost in IBD.

the cysteine-dependent regulation of the redox state in lamina propria lymphocytes is a key mechanism in the control of intestinal T cell homeostasis and that the cystine/cysteine redox couple represents a novel and potentially important therapeutic target in the treatment of IBD.

the redox state of lamina propria lymphocytes is controlled by the availability of cysteines, which in turn depends on the ability of the antigen-presenting cells in the intestinal microenvironments to release cysteines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cysteine availability is a critical factor regulating the proliferative capacity of LP-Ts in vitro and in vivo.
cystine is a critical limiting factor for the intracellular redox status of LP-Ts, thereby securing their physiological unresponsiveness in the intestinal micro-environment.

the capacity of lamina propria monocytes to reduce cystine to cysteine and thereby to promote proliferation of lamina propia T lymphocytes may represent a novel target for therapeutic intervention in IBD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LP-Ts are intrinsically hyporesponsive and require a specific microenvironmental signal for proliferation.
cysteine is a limiting factor for the proliferative potential of intestinal lamina propria CD4+ T cells.
the availability of cysteines is a critical factor that regulates the reactivity of T cells in the gut.
